title: Three Names
description: Shade a shape and name the shaded part three ways, as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent, all one amount.
modes: none. One flow, one phase at a time. The host mounts a phase (phase prop). With navigableDots true, or no phase, the child may jump phases with the dots (user mode); otherwise the dots show progress and the teacher agent drives window.toolApi (AI mode). The last phase, and a whole lesson, end on the summary page, where Free play and Play again sit. With navDots the dots are controls in AI mode too: a tap on a dot starts that phase.

stage.sizing: the frame is min(100vw, 177.78vh) wide and min(100vh, 56.25vw) tall (dvh where supported); the svg fills it. Nothing scrolls.

bands.header: 0 to 80. One line: the tool name, a measured dot, the phase concept; Hint, sound and restart as round controls far right.
bands.canvas: 92 to 640. One rounded card holding the key at its top right (Answer, Close, Enter, Next, or the Yes / No keys; no question bar), the working area (the whole card until Answer is tapped) and the answer drawer that slides in from the right; the summary page covers it at the end.
bands.footer: 652 to 900. The mascot at the far left on its ground line, the speech bubble beside it (y 656 to 892, the question and every line, printed), one small dot per phase at the right.

zones.layout: board, key only: no question bar, only its key at the right end of the top row (the question is on the bubble); the working area is the whole card (64, 108, 1472 x 520) until the child taps Answer, when the answer drawer (as tall as the working area, the key on its top row reading Close) slides in from the right
zones.controls: circles r 28 at cx 1388, 1460, 1532, cy 40: Hint (data-control again), sound, restart; 72-unit finger boxes
zones.dots: one small dot per phase at the footer's right (72-unit finger boxes, centred on the bubble), no text; in user AND AI mode each is a button (data-control phase-dot, data-phase k) that starts its phase

stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box on the stage. The score leaves on finished and onComplete and is shown once, as stars on the summary page.

writeup.why: Name a shaded part as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent, see all three as one amount, accept any equivalent fraction unless lowest terms are asked, start from a per cent, and say the chapter's words in the child's own terms.
writeup.look: A shape at the left, cut into equal parts and labelled Whole and 100%. The three name cards stand at its right, and on the last phase the word cards and the can-do cards.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Three Names' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many parts are shaded out of how many. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The shape stands inside a square 440 by 440 at x 110, y 230, labelled Whole and 100% above it: a bar of cells 440 long, a circle 440 across, or a square of small squares 440 on a side. Its parts are exactly equal, cut by near-black lines; shaded parts are deep blue and unshaded parts stay warm white. The Shape switch and the Parts buttons run in a row along y 690 from x 110, each labelled in words. The Fraction, Decimal and Per cent cards stand one above the other at x 640, y 240, x 640, y 360 and x 640, y 480, each 260 by 90 and labelled in words; they turn green together when all three name the shading. The Hundredths and Simplify buttons stand at x 940, y 240 and x 940, y 330, and when either works the words Both terms light vermilion over the Fraction card while the shading does not change. A grey 0 labelled Place holder appears on the Decimal card only where a zero holds a place open. On the fourth phase the word cards lie in a tray at x 110, y 230, their pictures stand at x 420, y 230, and the five can-do cards stand in a column at x 900, y 230, each with Yes, Almost and Not sure boxes. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a point key, a fraction bar key and a % key. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the tools of this chapter share them. The part the question gives, as shaded cells, a fraction, a decimal or an amount, is deep blue, labelled Given. The per cent, fraction or decimal the working reaches, and what is left after a part is used, is green, labelled Answer or Left. Both terms multiplied or divided by one number, and the times one hundred step before the % sign, are vermilion, labelled Both terms or Times 100. A unit fact that puts two amounts in one unit is violet, labelled Unit fact. The part used, taken away or not won is rose, labelled Used or Not won. The step, cell or number being worked on now is amber. A zero holding a place open inside a decimal is grey, labelled Place holder, and nothing else on the stage is ever grey. An unshaded cell of a whole stays warm white inside its near-black outline, the % sign is near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength rather than turning grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The shape shows the last shading, with its fraction, decimal and per cent in green beside it.

phases.win: the cards read 11/20, 0.55 and 55%, and all three turn green together
phases.does: counts the shaded parts, types the fraction, taps Hundredths, and reads the decimal and the per cent
phases.goal: a shaded part is named as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent, and all three are one amount
phases.says: Count the shaded parts and all the parts. Then find the hundredths.
phases.check: Away from the screen: half of a garden has been dug. Say that part three ways.
phases.feels: three cards lighting green together for one shading
phases.hands: Draw a shape on squared paper cut into two, four, five, ten, twenty or twenty-five equal parts, shade some, and write the shaded part three ways on three cards.
phases.tries: First rung: count all the parts. Second rung: count the shaded parts and write the fraction. Third rung: the same task with fewer parts shaded, before the question's own returns.

wrong.why: both counts are on the shape, and the unshaded parts are the other number seen
wrong.move: puts the shaded parts over the unshaded parts
wrong.screen: every part of the shape is numbered in turn, shaded and unshaded, and the last number is lit amber under the Fraction card

wrong.why: the numerator is the count of shaded parts, so it seems to go after the point
wrong.move: writes the decimal from the numerator alone, without making hundredths
wrong.screen: the Hundredths button pulses, and a second copy of the shape shades what the child's decimal names beside the first

phases.screen: a circle cut into 20 equal parts with 11 shaded, and the three cards blank
phases.soWhat: a shaded part is named as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent, and all three are one amount

phases.win: the Fraction card shows 22/50 and 11/25 side by side, with 0.44 and 44% under both
phases.does: taps Simplify, watches the shading stay still, and compares the two fractions
phases.goal: any equivalent fraction is right unless lowest terms are asked, and the HCF gives lowest terms
phases.says: Both fractions name the same shading. Which one is in lowest terms?
phases.check: Away from the screen: are two tenths and one fifth the same amount? How could you show it?
phases.feels: the fraction changing while the shading holds still
phases.hands: Shade the same part of two paper bars, one cut into more cells than the other, and write each as a fraction. Check that they are equal by growing both to hundredths.
phases.tries: First rung: find a number that divides both terms. Second rung: divide both and read the new fraction. Third rung: the same task with smaller terms, before the question's own returns.

wrong.why: answers are often printed in lowest terms, so that form seems to be the right one
wrong.move: calls a fraction wrong because it is not in lowest terms
wrong.screen: both fractions stand side by side over the same shading, each grown to the same hundredths, and both are lit green

wrong.why: each term was divided by something it shares with a smaller number
wrong.move: divides the two terms by different numbers
wrong.screen: the shape beside the child's fraction is shaded to it, plainly a different amount, and the two divisors are lit amber

phases.screen: a bar of 50 equal cells with 22 shaded, and the Fraction card reading 22/50
phases.soWhat: any equivalent fraction is right unless lowest terms are asked, and the HCF gives lowest terms

phases.win: nine small squares shaded, and the cards read 9/25, 0.36 and 36%
phases.does: watches the hundredths shade, taps Simplify, and types the decimal
phases.goal: a per cent is written over 100 and simplified for the fraction, and its hundredths give the decimal
phases.says: Out of a hundred first. Then make the fraction as simple as it goes.
phases.check: Away from the screen: how would you write fifty per cent as a fraction in lowest terms?
phases.feels: the shape filling to the per cent, then the fraction shrinking to lowest terms
phases.hands: Write a per cent over one hundred on a card, shade that many cells of a paper hundred grid, then simplify the fraction and write the decimal.
phases.tries: First rung: write the per cent over one hundred. Second rung: find the HCF of the two terms. Third rung: the same task with a per cent that is a count of tens, before the question's own returns.

wrong.why: tenths were the first decimals met, so ten feels like the bottom number
wrong.move: writes the per cent over ten instead of one hundred
wrong.screen: a second copy of the shape shades what the child's fraction names beside the per cent's own shading, far more, and the denominator is lit amber

wrong.why: the fraction over one hundred is right, so the job feels done

wrong.screen: the Simplify button pulses once, and the words lowest terms in the question are lit amber

phases.screen: a square of 25 equal small squares, empty, and the Per cent card reading 36%
phases.soWhat: a per cent is written over one hundred and simplified for the fraction, and its hundredths give the decimal

phases.win: each word card sits on its picture, and every can-do card carries the child's own tick
phases.does: drags each word card onto its picture, says the word in its own words, and ticks each can-do card

phases.feels: each word landing on the picture that shows it
phases.hands: Make three cards, per cent, percentage and equivalent fractions. Draw a picture for each: a hundred grid with some cells shaded, an amount written as a per cent, and two equal bars shaded alike.
phases.tries: First rung: place the per cent card. Second rung: place the percentage card. Third rung: the same task with two cards and two pictures, before all three return.

wrong.why: the two words sound almost the same
wrong.move: swaps the per cent card and the percentage card
wrong.screen: both pictures are lit in turn, and the meaning of each word is read under its picture, with the swapped cards kept where the child put them

phases.screen: three word cards, a hundred grid, two equal bars shaded alike, and the can-do cards
phases.soWhat: per cent means out of a hundred, a percentage is an amount written as a per cent, and equivalent fractions name the same amount

writeup.delight: On the first phase, the moment the last card is right, the three cards chime one after another and turn green together, and a thin green outline runs once around the shaded part.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet typed. On the first phase a circle cut into equal parts has some shaded, and the three cards are blank. On the second a bar of cells has some shaded, with the Fraction card already filled. On the third a square of small squares is empty and the Per cent card holds a per cent. On the fourth the three word cards wait in a tray beside their pictures, with the can-do cards under them. One thing moves, once: the first control the phase needs gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any shape, cut into any of the offered numbers of parts, with any parts shaded, and the three cards reading it. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on naming a shaded part three ways, lowest terms or not, starting from a per cent, and the chapter's words.
voiceLines: A shape, cut into equal parts, waiting to be named.
Count the shaded parts and all the parts. Then find the hundredths.
Both fractions name the same shading. Which one is in lowest terms?
Out of a hundred first. Then make the fraction as simple as it goes.
Put each word on its picture. Then tell it in your own words.
A new shape. Three names, one amount.
Free play. Shade any shape and read its three names.
Count the shaded parts and all the parts again.
Every shaded part had three names, and all three agreed.

observations.why: a fraction, a decimal and a per cent of one shading all name one amount.
observations.soWhat: a shaded part has three names, and each can be checked through hundredths.
observations.observe: All three cards turned green at the same moment.

observations.why: equivalent fractions name the same amount.
observations.soWhat: any equivalent fraction is right unless lowest terms are asked.
observations.observe: Simplify changed the Fraction card, and the shading stayed exactly as it was.

observations.why: per cent means out of a hundred.
observations.soWhat: starting from a per cent, write it over one hundred, then simplify.
observations.observe: Typing a per cent shaded that many hundredths of the shape, whatever its number of parts.

observations.why: each word names a different idea: out of a hundred, an amount written as a per cent, and two fractions of one amount.
observations.soWhat: the chapter's words can be said in the child's own terms and drawn.
observations.observe: Each word card fitted one picture best.

phases.screen: a circle cut into 20 equal parts with 11 shaded, and the three cards blank
phases.win: the cards read 11/20, 0.55 and 55%, and all three turn green together
phases.traceback: counts the shaded parts and all the parts, grows the fraction to hundredths, then writes the decimal or the per cent
ladder: The bottom number counts every part of the circle, shaded or not.
Look at the bottom number on the Fraction card.
Per cent counts out of 100, so look at the bottom number of 1/2.

phases.screen: a bar of 50 equal cells with 22 shaded, and the Fraction card reading 22/50
phases.win: the Fraction card shows 22/50 and 11/25 side by side, with 0.44 and 44% under both
phases.traceback: lays both fractions over the same shading and grows them to the same hundredths, or divides both terms by the HCF
ladder: Look at the shaded cells of the bar, then read each fraction against them.
Lowest terms means no number above 1 divides both terms.
Count the shaded parts and every part of the circle.

phases.screen: a square of 25 equal small squares, empty, and the Per cent card reading 36%
phases.win: nine small squares shaded, and the cards read 9/25, 0.36 and 36%
phases.traceback: writes the per cent over 100 and divides both terms by their HCF, or reads the hundredths as a decimal
ladder: Write 45 over 100, then divide both numbers as far as they go.
Per cent counts hundredths, not tenths.
Start from 64 over 100, then keep going to lowest terms.

phases.screen: three word cards, a hundred grid, two equal bars shaded alike, and the can-do cards
phases.win: each word card sits on its picture, and every can-do card carries the child's own tick
phases.traceback: rings the picture and puts the right word card under it, the child's choice untouched
ladder: Count how many of the 100 squares are shaded.
Look at the three amounts: only one is written with a % sign.
Look at where the shading ends on each bar.
Count the shaded parts for the top number.
Write the shaded count over the count of all the parts.
Multiply the top and the bottom by the number that makes the bottom 100.
The top number over 100 gives the two digits after the point.
Find what to multiply 2 by to make 100, then multiply the top by it too.
When the bottom is 100, the top number is the per cent.
Does dividing the top and the bottom by 2 change which cells are shaded?
Check whether this question asked for lowest terms at all.
Find the HCF of the shaded parts and all the parts.
Divide the top and the bottom by that HCF.
The bottom number is every part, shaded or not.
If you divide, divide the top and the bottom by one and the same number.
Find the HCF of 45 and 100.
Divide both 45 and 100 by their HCF.
Hundredths take two places after the point.
Fill the places after the point in order: tenths first, then hundredths.
Find a number that divides both 64 and 100 exactly.
Keep dividing both terms until no number above 1 divides both.
Think of what the % sign tells you about the 100 squares.
Pick the word that means out of a hundred, not the word for an amount.
One word names the % sign, and another names an amount written with it.
Say 90% out loud as an amount, then find the word that names such an amount.
Compare the two shaded lengths, then think what that says about the fractions.
Fractions that name the same amount have a word of their own.

onWrong.marks: Nothing is marked, nothing resets, no colour means good or bad. The child's answer stays; the pad re-opens after the traceback.
tracebacks: Phase 1: counts the shaded parts and all the parts, grows the fraction to hundredths, then writes the decimal or the per cent
Phase 2: lays both fractions over the same shading and grows them to the same hundredths, or divides both terms by the HCF
Phase 3: writes the per cent over 100 and divides both terms by their HCF, or reads the hundredths as a decimal
Phase 4: rings the picture and puts the right word card under it, the child's choice untouched

voice.opening: A shape, cut into equal parts, waiting to be named.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play: pick a shape and its parts, shade some, and read the three names.
voice.onMiss: the item's own miss line, then the phase's two ladder rungs, shown at once UNDER the pinned instruction and kept until the child acts again
voice.onFinish: Every shaded part had three names, and all three agreed.
voice.rules: Silent: nothing is spoken (no device speech, no recorded clips, no Tap to start cover). The speech bubble is the guide: every instruction and hint is one printed page, numbers as words. The lesson is action-driven in every mode: a guide step's instruction stays until the child does the act it names; a wrong act shows that step's hint under the pinned instruction, a wrong answer the next rung of its ladder, and the hint stays unchanged until the child acts again; a right answer's next question, a phase's next phase and the summary's rows follow by themselves after a short celebration. The header's Hint key shows the step's hint or the next rung on demand. What is heard is sound effects (Web Audio), switched by the sound button, on in every mode. In classroom mode nothing waits for a tap except the pieces of a long line (the blinking arrow; a tap, Enter, Space, ArrowRight or PageDown on the bubble shows the next piece), and a tap on the bubble when nothing waits is the teacher's skip.

guide.playsOn: guide steps on phase 1, 2, 3: the phase opens on its first instruction and waits for the child's act (getState guideStep, guideSteps, guideOn); the agent's check() performs the current step; the last act opens the first question. Other phases open on their printed teach lines, and a demo phase waits for the child's own act.

palette.rule: A content colour fills countable things only and chrome never borrows one; coloured numerals and words take a deeper ink of their colour (4.5:1).

toolQuestions.source: props.questions ?? props.additionalProps?.questions is read; the authored rows below keep their stage (fitHost returns null).

items.planQuestion: A circle is cut into 20 equal parts, and 11 are shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent.

question.en: What fraction of this circle is shaded?

items.planQuestion: A square is cut into 25 equal small squares, and 9 are shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent.

question.en: Name the shaded part of this square as a decimal.

items.planQuestion: A bar of 2 equal cells has 1 shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction, a decimal and a per cent.

question.en: What per cent of this bar is shaded?

ask.en: Shaded part as a per cent?

items.planQuestion: A bar of 50 equal cells has 22 shaded. Is the shaded part 22/50 or 11/25?

question.en: 22/50 simplifies to 11/25: which of them names the shaded part of the bar?

items.planAnswer: Both. 22/50 = 11/25, so each is right unless lowest terms are asked

items.planQuestion: A bar of 20 equal cells has 18 shaded. Write the shaded part as a fraction in lowest terms.

question.en: Write the shaded part of this bar as a fraction in lowest terms.

items.planAnswer: 9/10. The HCF of 18 and 20 is 2, and 18/20 = 9/10

items.planQuestion: A circle is cut into 50 equal parts, and 15 are shaded. Write the shaded part two ways as a fraction.

question.en: Name the shaded part of this circle as a fraction, in any terms you like.

items.planAnswer: Such as 15/50 and 3/10, since 15/50 = 3/10. Either is right

items.planQuestion: A field is 45% sown. What fraction in lowest terms, and what decimal, is sown?

question.en: A field is 45% sown: write the sown part as a fraction in lowest terms.

items.planQuestion: Write 8% as a fraction in lowest terms and as a decimal.
A garden is 64% planted. Write the planted part as a fraction in lowest terms and as a decimal.

question.en: A garden is 64% planted: what fraction in lowest terms is planted?

items.planQuestion: What does 37% mean, and is 37% a percentage?

question.en: Which word card tells what the % sign in 37% means?

items.planAnswer: 37 out of every hundred, which is 37/100. Yes, it is a percentage

items.planQuestion: Which of these is a percentage: 0.9, 9/10 or 90%?

question.en: Which word card names an amount written as a per cent, like 90%?

items.planAnswer: 90%, the amount written as a per cent. All three name one amount

items.planQuestion: Write two fractions equivalent to 3/10, and say what equivalent fractions are.

question.en: Which word card names two fractions like 3/10 and 6/20?

items.planAnswer: Such as 6/20 and 30/100. Equivalent fractions name the same amount

scoring.wrong: costs nothing, never marked, counted only for first try accuracy
scoring.stars: one for finishing, two at sixty per cent right first time, three at ninety; hidden with the first-try line by showScore false
scoring.phaseMount: a mount scores every phase it plays, from its phase to the last (+5 a question; phases of 3, 3, 3, 3 questions)
scoring.finishCard: stars and the Right first time line under the phase rows on the summary page

hostContract.phase: absent (not a finite number): the whole lesson, phases one to 4 in a row, the summary page at the end, finished once. Present: rounded and clamped to one to 4; the tool starts at that phase and, as the NCERT tools do, walks on by itself after each phase's last question (its closing line, then 1.4 s), in user and AI mode alike, through phase 4 to the summary page (a tool with nextKey, runtime r48+: in user mode it waits for the child's blinking Next key instead, after every question and every phase, and the last phase's key opens the summary; AI mode, and a host that mounts one phase without navigableDots, walk on by themselves); finished once, from the summary page.
hostContract.navigableDots: true (or no phase): user mode, the phase dots are controls; otherwise AI mode, the dots show progress and the agent drives window.toolApi.

onProgress.done: questions right so far in this phase

hostContract.emits: every event is dispatched on window and, when framed, posted to window.parent as { type: 'event', name, detail }

getState: toolId, mediaId, mode, mountPhase, phase, phases, conceptId, objectiveIds, step, steps, item, items, stage (teach, demo, ask, win, idle, summary, free), question, questionText, choices, typed, keypadOpen, tries, answered, firstTry, score, maxScore, answerShown (only after the answer), complete, questionCount, muted (the sound effects), speaking (always false: the lesson is silent), voice ("silent"), mascot, summaryRow, played, classroom, held (a classroom's parked piece of a long line), instruction (the pinned line), hint (the hint under it, or null), guideStep / guideSteps / guideOn (a guide-steps phase only), words, q, k, q

terminalEvent.name: finished
terminalEvent.fires: once per mount, from the summary page after the last phase, 5 s after the page opens (its lines may still be going on); one-shot guarded and re-armed by restart or Play again; never sent at the end of an earlier phase (the tool walks on), and never if Free play or Play again is tapped first

sounds: Web Audio, no files, on in every mode (the sound button switches them): correct, wrong (soft), win at a phase end, cheer at the last, a tick when a piece snaps, and cut, settle and trade where the picture moves
